preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the fixed-azimuth quarantine annotation with its paired precipitation deltas verbatim; it makes the thirty-second convective divergence visually separable from a sustained co-occurring transient in any year-three appendix read. The concrete design choice I advance: before the 1.5 mm/h threshold comparison, the system subtracts each gauge's last-certificate-to-present drift (tracked from the calibration log at every weekly certificate renewal) so the delta tests true spatial-temporal divergence rather than instrument error, and if the residual inter-gauge calibration uncertainty after subtraction exceeds 0.5 mm/h the quarantine annotation is replaced with "CAL-UNCERTAINTY DOMINANT — QUARANTINE SUPPRESSED — FRAME CLASSIFIED BY PRIMARY OPERATOR VISUAL ONLY, OFFSET FRAME ARCHIVED UNMATCHED," waiving the cross-reference obligation for that interval. The failure this subtraction and suppression rule closes: week 21, Site 2, the offset-tripod gauge has drifted +0.6 mm/h since its week-14 certificate while the primary gauge (week-2 certificate) holds, so a genuine 1.0 mm/h convective-spatial delta is recorded as 1.6 mm/h, trips the quarantine, and accumulates into an 18% weekly quarantine rate that exceeds the hypothetical 12% site-repositioning review threshold, sending an unnecessary survey crew to a geometry-adequate site while the real drift goes uncorrected because no annotation ever flagged the calibration state as the causal variable. The suppression annotation, carrying both certificate dates and the computed drift vector, lets the appendix reader reconstruct that the quarantine was an artifact and retroactively re-admit the offset frame into the decouled subsection under the primary operator's visual classification, preserving the convective transient's record without altering the site's geometry or the operator's interval schedule.

preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the drift-subtraction gate and the calibration-dominance suppression annotation verbatim; they correctly prevent instrument error from masquerading as spatial-temporal divergence and protect the site's geometry from false-positive repositioning triggers. The concrete design choice I advance: any suppression-annotation interval whose primary-operator visual classification marks the transient "present" must complete a three-instant temporal hold window at the site's native shutter cadence before the annotation finalizes, converting a single ambiguous frame into a short sustained sequence and closing the identification-metadata gap that suppression re-opens when the offset cross-reference is waived. The failure this holds against: week 34, Site 3, a forty-second squall delivers 2 mm/h, residual inter-gauge cal uncertainty after subtraction computes to 0.9 mm/h and triggers suppression, the operator squints at a grey smear and logs "present" with blank identification cells while rushing to the pressure reading, and because the squall clears before the second shutter instant the hold window never completes, so the annotation finalizes as "TRANSIENT < HOLD-WINDOW — SINGLE-FRAME VISUAL — NO OFFSET CROSS-REF — CAL-SUPPRESSION CERT [primary wk-18 / offset wk-22] — RUNNING Δ [0.9 mm/h]" and the record archives as provisional. A year-three appendix reader confronting that provisional annotation, the paired certificate dates, and the empty identification cell can correctly conclude the transient was too brief for confirmation, the cross-reference was legitimately waived under calibration dominance, and no confirmed weather event attaches to the interval; without the hold-window qualifier the identical blank-cell frame would be indistinguishable from a confirmed transient with simply omitted metadata, silently inflating the site's annual precipitation tally.

target.speaker: Y
target.text: I adopt the three-instant temporal hold window and its provisional-annotation finalization rule verbatim; it converts the single ambiguous frame into an interpretable episodic record that a year-three reader can correctly read as unconfirmed rather than silently confirmed. The concrete design choice I advance: every provisional annotation carries a hard 90-day expiration timestamp, after which the interval is silently reclassified "ABSENT — INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE — Δ-ZEROED" in the site's precipitation ledger, and the neighborhood weekly report aggregates confirmed-only totals from the confirmed ledger while publishing the unresolved-transient count per site as a separate appendix line item, so the provisional category never contaminates the confirmed tally nor vanishes from the audit trail. The failure this expiration-and-separation rule closes: week 3 through week 40, Site 4, a budget pressure gauge with a +0.7 mm/h weekly drift slope exceeds the 0.5 mm/h suppression threshold at nearly every precipitation interval, generating forty-one provisional annotations whose blank identification cells and suppressed cross-references accumulate into an annual "unresolved transient" count that a neighborhood comparison table renders visually indistinguishable from a site that genuinely experienced forty-one brief convective events, inflating Site 4's relative-activity ranking and triggering a spurious peer-review flag at the month-twelve summary while the true causal variable—the gauge drift slope—goes unaddressed because no annotation ever isolated it as the dominant term. The expiration rule zeroes the forty-one stale intervals from the confirmed ledger before any month-twelve comparison is printed, and the drift-slope surveillance metric computed at each weekly certificate renewal flags the +0.7 mm/h vector at week 8 with a mandatory gauge-replacement work order, so Site 4's week-9-through-week-40 intervals are recorded under a calibrated instrument and the month-twelve comparison table reflects true convective history rather than forty-one calibration artifacts.
